title: Is the default string field type in Elasticsearch `text` or `keyword`, and how does dynamic mapping handle it?
shortTitle: The default string field type in Elasticsearch — `text` or `keyword` — and how dynamic mapping handles it

s1_definition.profdef: When Elasticsearch encounters a string field it has never seen and you have not defined a mapping for it, dynamic mapping automatically maps it as a multi-field: the field itself is typed as `text`, which is analyzed for full-text search, and a sub-field named `keyword` is added, typed as `keyword`, which is stored verbatim for exact matching, sorting, and aggregations. So the honest answer is that neither is "the" single default — the default is both at once, with `text` as the main field and `keyword` as a sub-field (by default capped at 256 characters). The `text` type tokenizes and lowercases the value so you can search for words inside it, while the `keyword` type keeps the whole string unbroken so you can filter, sort, and group on the exact value.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India files a customer's full address. The bank keeps it in two forms. One form is chopped into searchable words — "street," "mumbai," "india" — so a clerk can find anyone living in Mumbai; that is the `text` form. The other form is the whole address kept exactly as written on one line, used when you need to match the precise address or group customers by it; that is the `keyword` form. When the bank first sees a new kind of field, it automatically files it in both forms, just in case you need to search inside it and also match it exactly.
s1_definition.oneliner: A new string field is dynamically mapped as `text` for searching words inside it, with a `.keyword` sub-field for exact match, sort, and aggregation — you get both unless you declare otherwise.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When Elasticsearch encounters a string field it has never seen and you have not defined a mapping for it, dynamic mapping automatically maps it as a multi-field: the field itself is typed as `text`, which is analyzed for full-text search, and a sub-field named `keyword` is added, typed as `keyword`, which is stored verbatim for exact matching, sorting, and aggregations. So the honest answer is that neither is "the" single default — the default is both at once, with `text` as the main field and `keyword` as a sub-field (by default capped at 256 characters). The `text` type tokenizes and lowercases the value so you can search for words inside it, while the `keyword` type keeps the whole string unbroken so you can filter, sort, and group on the exact value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India files a customer's full address. The bank keeps it in two forms. One form is chopped into searchable words — "street," "mumbai," "india" — so a clerk can find anyone living in Mumbai; that is the `text` form. The other form is the whole address kept exactly as written on one line, used when you need to match the precise address or group customers by it; that is the `keyword` form. When the bank first sees a new kind of field, it automatically files it in both forms, just in case you need to search inside it and also match it exactly.

**One line to remember:** A new string field is dynamically mapped as `text` for searching words inside it, with a `.keyword` sub-field for exact match, sort, and aggregation — you get both unless you declare otherwise.

sections.s2_technical:
To answer precisely you have to separate two things: what type a string becomes, and how dynamic mapping decides that. Dynamic mapping is the behaviour where, if you index a document containing a field that is not in the index's mapping, Elasticsearch infers a type from the value and adds it to the mapping automatically. For a JSON string value, the inferred result since version five is not a single type but a multi-field. The top-level field is mapped as `text`, and underneath it Elasticsearch adds a sub-field called `keyword` mapped as the `keyword` type, with an `ignore_above` setting of 256 so that strings longer than 256 characters are not indexed as a keyword, protecting against giant values bloating the index.

The `text` type is for full-text search. When a value is indexed into a text field it passes through an analyzer that tokenizes and normalizes it, so "International Wire Transfer" becomes the terms international, wire, and transfer. This lets a match query find the document when the user searches for any of those words regardless of case. But because the original value was broken into tokens, a text field by default cannot be used efficiently for sorting or for aggregations that group by the exact original value, and it does not support exact-equality filtering on the whole string.

The `keyword` type is the opposite. The value is stored as a single, exact, un-analyzed term. "International Wire Transfer" stays as that whole string. This is what you use for structured identifiers and categorical data: an account id, a status like SETTLED or FAILED, a currency code, a country. Keyword fields support exact-term filtering, sorting, and aggregations such as counting how many transactions are in each status, because grouping needs the whole unbroken value.

The reason dynamic mapping gives you both is that at the moment a new field first appears, Elasticsearch does not know your intent. You might want to search inside the text, or you might want to filter and aggregate on the exact value, or both. By creating the `text` field plus the `keyword` sub-field, it hedges: you reach the searchable form by the field name itself, and the exact form by appending dot keyword, for example querying the field for a match but aggregating on field dot keyword.

There is important nuance about which fields get this treatment. Dynamic mapping infers other JSON types too: a JSON number becomes a numeric type like long or float, a boolean becomes boolean, and a string that looks like a date can be mapped as a date if date detection is enabled, which is why a field containing "2026-10-25" might unexpectedly become a date rather than text. This date detection surprising people is a common gotcha. Dynamic mapping also has modes you can set per index: the default true adds new fields automatically, runtime adds them as runtime fields evaluated at query time, false ignores unknown fields but still stores them, and strict rejects documents containing unmapped fields, which is the safest choice for a production index where you want full control.

The senior-level guidance is that relying on dynamic mapping for a production index is convenient but risky, so experienced teams usually define explicit mappings. If every string automatically becomes text-plus-keyword, you can double your index size storing two representations of fields you only ever filter on, and you can get the wrong type when date detection misfires. For a banking audit index I would explicitly map an account id and a status as pure `keyword`, a free-text description as `text`, and a timestamp as a `date`, and I would often set dynamic to strict so an unexpected field in a document is rejected rather than silently and perhaps wrongly mapped. Dynamic mapping is excellent for exploration and for log data whose shape varies, but for a stable, performance-sensitive schema, explicit mapping is the professional default.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the team indexes transaction records with a free-text description, a status, and an account id. They first let dynamic mapping infer the types, then discover why explicit mapping is better.

Problem 1 — A support agent needs to search descriptions for the word "wire" and find every matching transaction. If the description were stored only as an exact keyword, searching for a single word inside it would fail. This is exactly why the description should be `text`: it is tokenized so word searches work.

Problem 2 — A dashboard needs to count transactions grouped by status, such as how many are SETTLED versus FAILED. If status were only `text`, it would be broken into tokens and could not be grouped by its exact value. This is exactly why status should be `keyword`: the whole value is kept for aggregation.

Problem 3 — Letting dynamic mapping map everything as text-plus-keyword wastes space on fields like the account id that are only ever filtered exactly, and risks mis-typing. This is exactly why the team moves to an explicit, strict mapping for the production index.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that models the two field behaviours. It will contain a `TextField` that analyzes values into tokens and supports word-level match, a `KeywordField` that stores values verbatim and supports exact match and grouping, a `DynamicMapper` that, for a new string field, creates a text field with a keyword sub-field, and an `ExplicitMapping` that lets you declare the right type per field. The demo indexes transactions both ways, runs a word search on the description, aggregates by status, and shows why explicit mapping is the production choice.
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
text-keyword-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/fields/
│   │   │   ├── FieldDemo.java                     (main class)
│   │   │   ├── field/
│   │   │   │   ├── TextField.java                  (analyzed, word search)
│   │   │   │   └── KeywordField.java               (verbatim, exact + group)
│   │   │   ├── mapping/
│   │   │   │   ├── DynamicMapper.java              (auto text + .keyword)
│   │   │   │   └── ExplicitMapping.java            (declared types)
│   │   │   └── model/
│   │   │       └── Transaction.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── application.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/fields/
│           └── mapping/
│               └── MappingTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml — the explicit mapping we want in production
index:
  name: transactions
  dynamic: strict           # reject unmapped fields in production
  properties:
    description: text        # searchable words
    status: keyword          # exact match + aggregation
    account_id: keyword      # identifier, never tokenized
    created_at: date
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the model
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/text-keyword-demo-1.0.0.jar

# Real Elasticsearch: dynamic gives text + .keyword automatically.
# Word search uses the field; aggregation uses the .keyword sub-field:
curl -X GET "localhost:9200/transactions/_search" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"query":{"match":{"description":"wire"}},
       "aggs":{"by_status":{"terms":{"field":"status.keyword"}}}}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions, two describing international wire transfers with different casing, with statuses SETTLED, SETTLED, and FAILED.

Step 1: The DynamicMapper is asked about a new string field "description." It records "description" as text and adds "description.keyword" as a keyword with the 256-character cap, exactly reproducing how Elasticsearch dynamically maps a fresh string field into a multi-field.

Step 2: The text field indexes each description. "International Wire transfer" is lowercased and split into the tokens international, wire, transfer. The other two descriptions are tokenized the same way, so TXN-3's "international wire incoming" yields international, wire, incoming.

Step 3: A word search for "wire" runs against the text field. It lowercases the query and finds every document whose token set contains "wire," returning TXN-1 and TXN-3. This works precisely because text fields are analyzed into words; searching inside the string is possible.

Step 4: The keyword field indexes each status verbatim: SETTLED, SETTLED, FAILED, with no tokenization. An exact term query for "FAILED" returns only TXN-3, matching the whole unbroken value.

Step 5: A terms aggregation groups by exact status value and counts each group, producing SETTLED mapped to two and FAILED mapped to one. This works precisely because keyword fields keep the whole value, which is what grouping requires; a text field could not do this correctly because it would have split the values into tokens.

Step 6: The explicit production mapping is defined, assigning description to text, status and account id to keyword, and created_at to date — each field exactly the type it needs with no wasted dual representation. Finally the demo tries to index a field that is not in the mapping, and because the mapping is strict, that field is rejected, demonstrating the safety of controlling the schema rather than letting dynamic mapping guess.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 3:00:21 AM com.bank.fields.mapping.DynamicMapper onNewStringField
INFO: dynamically mapped 'description' -> text, 'description.keyword' -> keyword
INFO: search description for 'wire' -> [TXN-1, TXN-3]
INFO: term status='FAILED' -> [TXN-3]
INFO: aggregate by status -> {SETTLED=2, FAILED=1}
INFO: production mapping -> {description=text, status=keyword, account_id=keyword, created_at=date}
WARNING: strict mapping: unmapped field 'unexpected_field' rejected
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  New string field indexed (dynamic mapping)
    "International Wire transfer"
      │
      ├──→ field "description" : TEXT
      │       analyzer → [international, wire, transfer]
      │       supports: match(word)  → TXN-1, TXN-3
      │
      └──→ sub-field "description.keyword" : KEYWORD (ignore_above 256)
              stored verbatim: "International Wire transfer"
              supports: term(exact), sort, aggregate

  Status field
    "SETTLED","SETTLED","FAILED"  →  KEYWORD
      ├─ term("FAILED")         → {TXN-3}
      └─ aggregate (group by)   → {SETTLED:2, FAILED:1}

  Production: explicit + strict mapping
    description→text, status→keyword, account_id→keyword, created_at→date
    unknown field  →  REJECTED (strict)
```

  ┌─ Design Insight ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ + match(word)        │        │ + term(exact)            │
  │   (analyzed tokens)  │        │ + aggregate()            │

  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   DynamicMapper       │        │   ExplicitMapping        │
  │ + onNewStringField()  │        │ - strict: boolean        │
  │   → text + .keyword   │        │ + define(field,type)    │
  └──────────────────────┘        │ + indexDocumentField()  │

  1. DynamicMapper.onNewStringField("description") → text + .keyword
  2. TextField.match("wire") → {TXN-1, TXN-3}
  3. KeywordField.term("FAILED") → {TXN-3}

sections.s6_takeaway:
The precise answer is that neither `text` nor `keyword` alone is the default for a string in Elasticsearch — the default produced by dynamic mapping is both at once. When Elasticsearch meets a string field it has not seen and you have not defined, dynamic mapping creates a multi-field: the top-level field is mapped as `text`, which is analyzed for full-text search, and under it a sub-field named `keyword` is added, mapped as the `keyword` type with an ignore-above setting of 256 so overly long strings are not indexed as a keyword. So out of the box you can both search for words inside the value using the field name and match, sort, or aggregate on the exact value using the field name followed by dot keyword.

The two types exist because they do opposite jobs. A `text` field is analyzed — tokenized and lowercased — so "International Wire transfer" becomes the terms international, wire, and transfer, which is what lets a match query find the document when a user searches for any of those words regardless of case. But because the value was broken into tokens, a text field cannot by default be used for exact-equality filtering, sorting, or aggregating on the whole original value. A `keyword` field is the reverse: the whole value is stored verbatim and un-analyzed, which is exactly what you need for identifiers and categorical data like an account id, a status such as SETTLED or FAILED, or a currency code, because exact filtering and grouping require the unbroken value.

Dynamic mapping hedges by giving you both because, at the instant a new field first appears, Elasticsearch does not know your intent. It also infers other types — numbers become numeric, booleans become boolean, and a string that looks like a date can be mapped as a date if date detection is on, which is a common and surprising gotcha. And it has modes: the default true adds new fields automatically, false stores but ignores them, and strict rejects documents with unmapped fields entirely.

In production I treat dynamic mapping as convenient for exploration and for variable-shaped log data, but I define explicit mappings for stable, performance-sensitive indices. At National Bank of India, for the transactions audit index I explicitly mapped the description as `text` so support could search words inside it, the status and account id as `keyword` so dashboards could aggregate and compliance could filter exactly, and the timestamp as a `date`. I usually set dynamic to strict as well, so an unexpected field in a document is rejected rather than silently and perhaps wrongly mapped — for example a date-looking string sneaking in as a date. Relying on the automatic text-plus-keyword default everywhere would have doubled the index size storing two representations of fields I only ever filtered on, so controlling the schema explicitly was the professional choice.
